title: Woman Of The Year

jokes.text: Leslie mediates a dispute between adult coaches behaving like children, then immediately undercuts her own authority by saying 'no matter how boring the sport'
jokes.setup: Leslie positions herself as the mature adult peacemaker telling coaches they're role models
jokes.punchline: She adds 'no matter how boring the sport' — instantly undermining her diplomatic stance with her own personal disdain
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie Knope character comedy — she has strong convictions about fairness but can't suppress her own opinions even when being diplomatic. The self-undermining qualifier lands well because it's so specific to her.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.line: We need to act like adults here.

dialogue.speaker: Other Coach
dialogue.line: You're right, you're absolutely right.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.line: Your coaching is terrible and everyone knows it.

jokes.text: Leslie assumes the girls' coach is male and the boys' coach is female — 'Oh. Okay. Sorry. That's sexist.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is on a feminist crusade to get the girls' team a field
jokes.punchline: She immediately makes a sexist assumption about which coach is which — the feminist makes a sexist mistake
jokes.explanation: Well-earned irony. The joke works on two levels: it's funny in the moment and also genuinely insightful about how even well-meaning people carry implicit biases. The quick 'Yeah. Kind of is.' agreement from a bystander adds a nice button. Strong character integration — Leslie's passionate advocacy creating her own contradiction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wow, you two really handled that maturely. I'm so impressed by how you both communicated your feelings like adults.

jokes.text: Leslie ends her speech with 'And that, little lady, is a Leslie Knope promise!' — directed at what turns out to be a boy
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers a triumphant, folksy promise to a child she assumes is a girl
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a boy.' — the dramatic moment collapses
jokes.explanation: Classic tag-beat structure — the triumphant speech deflated by a single four-word line. The joke is tight and well-constructed. Leslie's recovery ('Good. Yeah. 'Cause I wasn't talking to you.') is an equally strong button that shows her inability to admit a mistake. This is a minor running theme for her character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Children are our future, and we need to protect their rights to education, safety, and opportunity. We need to invest in programs that give them access to sports, arts, and activities that inspire them. Though honestly, soccer is boring as hell.

jokes.text: Leslie recovers: 'Good. Yeah. 'Cause I wasn't talking to you. I was talking to you. You're a girl, right?'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been embarrassed by calling a boy 'little lady'
jokes.punchline: Rather than apologize, she digs in — confirming with the next child that they are, in fact, a girl before continuing
jokes.explanation: The button on the previous joke. Leslie's refusal to acknowledge her error and her overcorrection (now confirming gender before proceeding) is deeply in character. 'Yeah. She.' at the end as additional confirmation is a nice final beat showing her paranoia.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'll make the potato salad and you can grill the burgers.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.line: Why would I grill the burgers?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because you're a man.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.line: That's sexist.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No it's not, it's just how things are.

dialogue.speaker: Coach
dialogue.line: You just told me to do something based solely on my gender. That's the definition of sexism.

jokes.text: Jerry spills soup on the mail, and the group's immediate response is to berate him — 'Jerry! You got soup all over our mail! You jerk.'
jokes.setup: Mail arrives, seemingly a mundane moment
jokes.punchline: Jerry has ruined it through clumsiness, and the response is immediate and disproportionate contempt
jokes.explanation: Functional running gag — Jerry as the office scapegoat. The joke relies on established character dynamics rather than clever writing. 'You jerk' lands because it's so casually cruel. Works but isn't special.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hey there, little guy! How are you doing today?

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: I'm actually a girl.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my gosh, I am so sorry! Of course you are. You're such a beautiful young man.

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: You just did it again.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, well, I think I hear your mom calling you... over there... away from me.

jokes.text: 'Nobody freak out!' followed immediately by 'I am Pawnee's Woman of the Year!'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells everyone not to freak out
jokes.punchline: She then immediately freaks out by making a triumphant declaration before anyone has read the letter
jokes.explanation: Leslie telling people not to freak out while being the one freaking out is classic Leslie Knope character comedy. The speed of the pivot from 'stay calm' to triumphant announcement is the joke's engine. Her certainty that she's won before anyone has confirmed it sets up the humiliation payoff beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I was just trying to heat up some soup in the break room...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, why is there soup all over the mail?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I don't know! I was holding the bowl and the stack of envelopes at the same time and—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're an idiot.

jokes.text: Leslie in confessional: 'Winning is every girl's dream. But it's my destiny. And my dream.'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains the importance of the IOW award in a talking head
jokes.punchline: She starts with the universal ('every girl's dream'), then immediately claims individual ownership ('my destiny'), then doubles back to also claim the dream category ('And my dream')
jokes.explanation: Small but sharp character moment. The self-correction to also claim 'my dream' after she's already claimed 'my destiny' is a lovely bit of Leslie-ness — her ambition is so total she needs to own every superlative. Well-paced for a confessional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I joined a women's organization as a child.

jokes.text: The IOW award letter reveals the winner is 'Ronald Swanson'
jokes.setup: Leslie has built up enormous anticipation that she is Pawnee's Woman of the Year; everyone in the office is gathered around
jokes.punchline: The winner is Ron Swanson — a man, and Leslie's polar opposite in terms of values
jokes.explanation: The episode's primary comedic premise, delivered as a perfectly structured reveal. The setup is built over a full minute and a half with Leslie's escalating certainty. The punchline is Ron — a man who hates government awards, hates women's organizations, and is Leslie's ideological opposite — winning a feminist award. Character integration is near-perfect: no other two characters in the show could make this joke land as hard. The premise is original and the structure is textbook. This is the episode's anchor joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I can't believe Ron won the women's award!

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: It turns out I'm more of a woman than any of you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I have two X chromosomes, Leslie. I checked.

jokes.text: Leslie's reaction: 'Ha-ha. Okay, pretty funny. It says Ronald Swanson. What? No, no. No, it doesn't. I... That... No. That... What?'
jokes.setup: Leslie hears that Ron has won the Woman of the Year award
jokes.punchline: Her denial cascades through several stages — first assuming it's a joke, then trying to contradict facts, then just verbal breakdown
jokes.explanation: Amy Poehler's performance carries this, but the writing supports it well — the escalating breakdown from 'pretty funny' through logical denial to verbal static is perfectly structured. The fragmented 'I... That... No. That... What?' is a great comedic landing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, your mustache is falling off.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you're not okay.

jokes.text: Colleague: 'They only honor women. And Ron's the opposite of a woman.'
jokes.setup: Someone is explaining the confusion about Ron winning a women's award
jokes.punchline: 'And Ron's the opposite of a woman' — delivered as pure factual statement
jokes.explanation: Clean deadpan observation. The economy is the joke — 'the opposite of a woman' is both physically and philosophically true of Ron, and saying it with no editorializing is funnier than any elaboration would be.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Of course I won it. I'm Ron Swanson.

jokes.text: Ron, on hearing he won Woman of the Year: 'Well, it's about time.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just been told he's won a women's award from an organization he presumably despises
jokes.punchline: Rather than confusion or protest, complete deadpan acceptance as if long overdue
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Four words, maximum impact. The joke works on multiple layers: Ron's massive ego, his indifference to the absurdity of the situation, and the implicit suggestion that he considers himself superior to all categories of people. Only Ron Swanson says this. The economy is essentially perfect — one word more would ruin it. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor example.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was offered a citizen of the year award, which I promptly declined.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: However, I've decided to accept it. Not because I believe in recognition or awards, but solely to mess with Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The look on her face will be worth any amount of pretentious ceremony.

jokes.text: Ron's confessional: 'Awards are stupid, which is why I fully intend to decline this nonsense, and recommend it go to Leslie because she works really hard, and I don't.'
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining his plan to decline the award on principle
jokes.punchline: He casually admits 'and I don't' (work hard) as if it's a morally neutral statement
jokes.explanation: Ron's anti-work philosophy stated baldly and without apology. The structure of the sentence — a compliment to Leslie immediately undercut by a self-deprecating admission that's actually a brag — is elegant. Very Ron: generous in intention, completely honest about his own laziness.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Freddy, I got some good news for you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You just got got, yo.

jokes.text: Ron's confessional continues: 'However, she cares way too much about crap like this, which is why I can't pass up this opportunity to tease her about it.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just said he plans to give the award to Leslie
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to planning to torment her with it first — and delivers this as a completely reasonable decision
jokes.explanation: The two-part confessional (jokes 12 and 13) together constitute one of the episode's best sequences. This second beat reveals Ron's genuine affection for Leslie expressed through trolling. His logic is impeccable within his own worldview — he wants her to have it, but she must suffer first. Deeply in character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm opening my own club. I've been working on some names. What do you think of 'The Subsurface'?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Or 'Depth Charge'? 'The Mariana'? 'Crush Depth'?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've got like fifty submarine-themed club names.

jokes.text: Tom to a bar owner: 'Hey, Freddy. Good news! Your liquor license renewal got got, yo.'
jokes.setup: Tom is delivering official news about a liquor license
jokes.punchline: 'Got got, yo' — Tom using slang so awkwardly it becomes its own punchline
jokes.explanation: Tom's affected hip-hop inflection applied to bureaucratic government business is a reliable character note. 'Got got, yo' is specifically funny because of how unnecessary and confused the slang is even within Tom's own dialect.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What about 'The Bistro'? Bistro is inherently classy. You could have the worst food in the world, you could serve nothing but gas station sushi and—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, no, if it's called a bistro, people will think it's fancy.

jokes.text: Tom's club name brainstorm: 'Club-a-Dub-Dub, The Clubmarine (sort of a submarine-themed club), or Tom's Bistro. The word bistro is classy as.'
jokes.setup: Tom is pitching his future nightclub dreams
jokes.punchline: The names escalate from silly to sillier ('Club-a-Dub-Dub') then land on 'Tom's Bistro' with 'bistro is classy as' — the sentence ending without finishing its thought
jokes.explanation: 'Classy as' with nothing after it is a nice verbal tic — Tom's language sometimes outpaces his thoughts. The submarine-themed club is also a good absurdist detail. The list structure (three names escalating in pretension) works well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I'm gonna be honest with you. I didn't get into public service because I wanted to help people. I got into it because I thought it would be good for my business connections and help me network my way to success.

jokes.text: 'Or Tom's Bistro. The word "bistro" is classy as.'
jokes.setup: Tom has named two absurd club names; now he offers his 'classy' alternative
jokes.punchline: 'Tom's Bistro' with the defense 'The word bistro is classy as' — the sentence trails off, implying 'classy as [anything]' but more likely the F-word, making this simultaneously a half-finished thought and a confident declaration
jokes.explanation: The truncated 'classy as' is a great economy joke — the incomplete sentence implies vulgarity while maintaining Tom's aspiration to sophistication. It's also absurd that Tom's 'classy' option is just his own name plus a French word. The joke works on multiple registers: Tom's narcissism, his pseudo-sophistication, and the truncated profanity implication. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ten grand? That's it? I thought you were gonna ask for real money. I've spent more than that on a single lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what, I'm gonna need to think about it.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I agree. That's why I got into public service. To help me.'
jokes.setup: Freddy tells Tom he'd make a great asset to the club investment because of his 'political connections'
jokes.punchline: Tom confirms this assessment but reveals his entirely self-serving motivation for having those connections
jokes.explanation: One of Tom's best character lines in the episode. The admission is complete and delivered without shame. 'To help me' — three syllables, zero irony from Tom's perspective. The economy here is exceptional and the character integration is total: this is Tom's entire ethos.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so here's what we're gonna do. First, we contact the President. Then we get the Supreme Court involved. Then we hire a team of lawyers, the best lawyers, maybe even go international with this thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We could also start a petition, get a million signatures, maybe stage a peaceful protest right here in the Parks Department.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm thinking we go on every news network. Cable, network, international broadcasting. We make this the biggest story of the year.

jokes.text: Tom: '$10,000. That's chump change.' — then cut to confessional where it clearly is not chump change
jokes.setup: Freddy names a $10,000 price for a share of the club
jokes.punchline: Tom dismisses it as chump change — implying he has it — then his subsequent scrambling to find the money reveals he absolutely does not
jokes.explanation: A classic bravado-then-reality structure. Works efficiently as scene transition comedy. Tom's posturing is immediately undercut by the subsequent plot of desperately scrounging for money.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: My grandfather died? That's the best news I've heard all week! I'm gonna be rich!

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Finally, all those years of him ignoring me are gonna pay off. This is gonna be awesome!

jokes.text: Leslie's to-do list: 'Write an e-mail to Barack Obama. Lock myself in my office and scream until I lose my voice.'
jokes.setup: Ann suggests Leslie should 'do something' about the award situation
jokes.punchline: Leslie already has a list — but it goes from completely ineffectual (emailing the President for an IOW award dispute) to cathartic rage (screaming until voiceless)
jokes.explanation: A lovely character joke that tells us everything about Leslie. The Barack Obama email is both absurdly over-escalated and completely believable for her — she genuinely thinks he'd want to help. The scream option shows her emotional state. The list format and the 'That's all I have so far' creates a nice open-endedness suggesting more deranged options are forthcoming.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm really sorry to hear about your grandfather, Jean-Ralphio.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Thanks, but honestly, he was a terrible person. He used to steal from me and my brother constantly.

jokes.text: Leslie tries repeatedly to say 'Hey, Ann' and get Ann's attention while Jean-Ralphio interrupts — 'Jean-Ralphio. Big T! What it do, nephew?'
jokes.setup: Leslie urgently needs to talk to Ann
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio sweeps in and monopolizes Tom's attention, Ann redirects Leslie through intermediary — the urgency is deflated by pure chaos
jokes.explanation: More of a scene-setting moment than a pure joke. 'What it do, nephew?' is distinctly Jean-Ralphio but the comedic interruption structure is relatively standard.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: My trust fund is gonna be huge. I'm gonna buy a dolphin and keep it in my pool. Then I'm gonna teach it to do backflips and shit. And then when I get tired of it, I'm gonna eat it.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio: 'Hit me with it, daddy.' — responding to Tom's investment pitch
jokes.setup: Tom says he has a hot investment opportunity
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's response is a bizarre blend of enthusiasm and questionable slang — 'daddy' as an affectionate term for his financial partner
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's language is consistently a joke delivery system. 'Daddy' is the specific word doing the work here — bizarre and slightly uncomfortable in context.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy is the worst roommate. He leaves dishes everywhere, he's loud at all hours, and I'm pretty sure he's been conducting some kind of experiment with a Bag of Smells in the closet.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio: '...my grandfather just died, so I am flush with cash!'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is explaining why he can suddenly invest
jokes.punchline: Grandfather's death revealed as purely good news — the 'a-' stammer before 'flush' suggests he almost said something worse — delivered with complete elation
jokes.explanation: The dark humor here is perfectly calibrated. The 'a-' stutter before 'flush' suggests he almost said 'awash' or something more revealing, and the exclamation point delivery makes his inappropriate joy the punchline. Tom's near-immediate 'Also, sorry about your grandpa' pivot makes it even better — treating the death as an afterthought.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You need to stop this. It's disgusting.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, I'm conducting a scientific experiment. This bag contains specimens from every smell in the world.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It contains old gym socks and a rotting sandwich.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Exactly. And look at these results. Day one: nausea. Day two: hallucinations. Day three: I'm pretty sure I can see sounds now.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio: 'No worries. He was a dick.'
jokes.setup: Tom offers a belated condolence about Jean-Ralphio's grandfather
jokes.punchline: 'No worries. He was a dick.' — complete dismissal with no elaboration
jokes.explanation: Four words, very high impact. The callback to the grandfather, and Jean-Ralphio's breezy characterization of a dead family member as simply 'a dick,' is perfect dark comedy. Economy score is near-perfect — nothing can be added or removed. Highly quotable and lands harder on rewatch knowing Jean-Ralphio's character.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: My roommate is completely controlling. He monitors everything I do.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: He won't let me use the microwave after 8 PM, he color-codes the refrigerator, and he has a detailed spreadsheet of whose turn it is to buy toilet paper.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But here's the thing that really gets me — every night around midnight, he goes out to the backyard with a shovel and just... digs. For hours.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I asked him what he's digging for and he just stares at me and says, 'You wouldn't understand, Andy. You don't have the vision.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: There's a hole in our backyard that's now eight feet deep and shaped like a perfect triangle. I'm pretty sure he's either burying bodies or training for some kind of weird Olympic sport.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's trust fund situation: 'I don't get anything until I'm 50, which is a waste, 'cause I'm gonna be a billionaire in Costa Rica by then, eating dolphins and hanging out with lady singers.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio explains he can't access his trust fund
jokes.punchline: His reasoning for why this is wasteful includes a bizarrely specific future: billionaire, Costa Rica, eating dolphins, 'lady singers'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Eating dolphins' is a genuinely unexpected and specific absurdist choice — not 'partying' or 'living large,' but the particular image of eating dolphins alongside 'lady singers.' The specificity creates the comedy. This is a deeply Jean-Ralphio sentence — no other character would have this exact vision. The detail is weird enough to earn a genuine laugh from sophisticated viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, the band broke up? Oh no!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Actually, we didn't break up. We just changed our name.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, that's great! What's the new name?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Scaramouche Scaramouche Will You Do the Fandango.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's... worse than the original name.

jokes.text: Andy is living with his band's guitarist and the grievances include 'The Bag of Smells' — 'No. We're finally starting to get serious results.'
jokes.setup: Andy's roommate is listing complaints about living with Andy
jokes.punchline: 'The Bag of Smells was a fun experiment but it has to stop' / 'We're finally starting to get serious results' — Andy treats a bag of smells as a legitimate scientific endeavor
jokes.explanation: 'The Bag of Smells' is a fantastically specific and original piece of absurdist character comedy. We don't know what it is — we don't need to. The name alone is funny. Andy's defense that they are 'getting serious results' from a bag of smells is the perfect escalation. Pure Andy Dwyer — chaotic, committed, and completely unapologetic.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You're like a beautiful flower that blooms in the darkness.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Flowers need sunlight to bloom.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, it's poetic.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's not poetic, it's botanically incorrect.

jokes.text: You wanna come home with me? / Don't you work at Lady Foot Locker? / Look, if you're not gonna pay rent, at least clean up your dishes.
jokes.setup: Andy is apparently crashing at April's place. She invites him somewhere.
jokes.punchline: His response to her invitation is to ask if she works at Lady Foot Locker — a completely non-sequitur response that implies he's had a very different conversation in his head. Then she snaps back to the actual issue: he's not paying rent.
jokes.explanation: The Lady Foot Locker non-sequitur is odd enough to be genuinely funny — it suggests Andy has been internally processing something completely unrelated. April's pragmatic pivot grounds the scene. Solid character work for both.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, you realize you're in a women's organization, right? That's like me joining a group called 'Guys Who Think Government is a Waste of Money' and then being surprised when they don't want to help me fix a pothole.

jokes.text: Andy quotes his guitarist's complaints including: 'That's not a working fireplace, Andy.' 'Stop writing phone messages on the wall, Andy.' 'Dude, seriously, I love you but stop digging that weird hole in the backyard.'
jokes.setup: Andy is complaining about his controlling guitarist roommate
jokes.punchline: Each grievance reveals something weirder about Andy — the 'weird hole' in the backyard caps the escalating list
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured escalating list joke. Each item is funny and specific ('not a working fireplace,' 'writing phone messages on the wall'), building to the magnificent 'weird hole in the backyard.' The rule of three is executed with precision. The guitarist's 'I love you but...' softener on the final item adds a human touch. All three grievances are individually funny and together paint a complete, absurd portrait of living with Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What was that project you were working on? The Pawnee... the Pawnee...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The Pawnee Commons?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes, the Pawnee Commons. I was very close.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Is Mouse Rat gonna break up?' / 'Well, we're not Mouse Rat anymore. We changed it to Tackleshaft.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks if Mouse Rat (Andy's band) will break up due to tension
jokes.punchline: Andy reveals the band is fine, but they've changed their name to 'Tackleshaft' — which is somehow even worse than Mouse Rat
jokes.explanation: 'Tackleshaft' is a perfect fake band name — aggressive, nonsensical, and somehow more embarrassing than Mouse Rat. The reveal works because the audience is expecting breakup drama, and instead gets a mundane name change to something objectively terrible. Andy is clearly unbothered by this.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I appreciate the gesture, but I have to be honest - I didn't earn this award on my own merits.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie made me look good enough to win it.

jokes.text: Andy to April: 'April, you're like an angel with no wings.' / April: 'So, like, a person?'
jokes.setup: Andy offers April a sweet, poetic compliment
jokes.punchline: April deflates it with literal logic — an angel without wings is just a person
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best joke. Five words — 'So, like, a person?' — that do extraordinary work. The structure is flawless: Andy's earnest romantic poetry is demolished by April's deadpan literalism. It's character comedy at its highest — this exact exchange could ONLY happen between these two specific characters. Andy's sweetness and April's affect together create a comedic tension that pays off perfectly. The joke has become a fan-favorite quotable moment from the series. Economy is nearly perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, little boy, I know you're upset about the field, but—

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: I'm a girl.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, yes, of course you are. Now, as I was saying, sweetie...

jokes.text: Ron's response to Leslie's complaint: 'Really? You're saying a women's organization made a mistake?'
jokes.setup: Leslie argues the IOW made a mistake giving the award to Ron
jokes.punchline: Ron's sarcastic 'Really?' frames the irony — a women's organization, of all groups, made an error favoring a man over a woman
jokes.explanation: Ron's pleasure in the irony is palpable. The line is economical and uses the situation's inherent comedy well. He's not actively mean — just enjoying the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know, a dress code is like life. You gotta follow the rules, but you also gotta make it work for you. That's why I'm wearing this Tom Ford suit with these Gucci loafers and this Hermès belt. I'm following the rules, but I'm doing it in style.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Hmm. Well, it definitely said Ron Swanson in the letter.' / Leslie: 'Yeah, but it also mentioned my camp project.' / Ron: 'Yes. Camp Xena.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to prove the award should be hers because it mentions her project
jokes.punchline: Ron gets the camp name wrong — 'Camp Xena' vs 'Camp Athena' — revealing he has zero investment in the details of her work
jokes.explanation: 'Camp Xena' is a specifically funny wrong answer — not completely off, which would be too easy, but close enough to be insulting. The name mangle is believable as Ron's casual dismissiveness and works as character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I did a portrait shoot for the Pawnee newspaper. It's called IOW—Images of Women.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You mean IUD?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, IOW. Images of Women.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's an intrauterine device.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You deserve an award. Not this one, obviously, this one belongs to me, but some other one. Some other lesser award.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to tell Ron she's not angry at him personally
jokes.punchline: Her compliment immediately qualifies itself into an insult — the award Ron deserves would be 'lesser'
jokes.explanation: Nice self-undermining compliment. The qualifiers pile up hilariously — 'Not this one, obviously, this one belongs to me, but some other one.' Leslie's competitive nature overwhelms her attempt at graciousness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Should I hold a frying pan or a briefcase for my official portrait?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, those are both sexist stereotypes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. That's why I'm asking you to help me pick which one.

jokes.text: Ron: 'And if the shoe were on the other foot and you won the award, I would've congratulated you.' — Leslie immediately says: 'Congratulations, Ron.'
jokes.setup: Ron implies Leslie should congratulate him since he would do the same
jokes.punchline: Leslie congratulates him deadpan — then Ron: 'What's that?' / Leslie: 'You heard me.'
jokes.explanation: Great comedic rhythm. Leslie grits her teeth and delivers the congratulations, Ron can't believe it and asks her to repeat it, and 'You heard me' makes clear she's not saying it again. It's a perfect two-character exchange that shows both people completely — Leslie's reluctant compliance, Ron's surprise and satisfaction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Help me win my award!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's what you're doing, Barbie. You're helping me win my award.

jokes.text: Leslie directs a youth soccer player to Ron: 'He's an award-winning public servant. He's the guy that's gonna help you out.'
jokes.setup: A youth sports figure has a problem about field access
jokes.punchline: Leslie, who can't deal with Ron right now, redirects him — with bitter sarcasm — to the 'award-winning' Ron Swanson
jokes.explanation: A functional callback. 'Award-winning public servant' carries Leslie's barely suppressed fury. Works as character comedy and situation irony.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you won an award. Shouldn't that make you humble?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No. I won an award because I'm excellent. And everything I do is excellent. Which is why I won the award. It's a perfect circle.

jokes.text: Tom's VIP card pitch with the line: 'Dress code? Black tie optional. Just like life.'
jokes.setup: Tom is handing out VIP cards for his investment pitch
jokes.punchline: 'Black tie optional. Just like life.' — an utterly meaningless but delivered-with-conviction philosophical non sequitur
jokes.explanation: 'Just like life' makes absolutely no sense as a follow-up to 'black tie optional' and Tom delivers it as profound wisdom. The confidence-to-content ratio is perfect Tom Haverford. Short, quotable, and tells you everything about who he thinks he is.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So what are you looking for in an apartment?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I need a doorman named either Frank or Steve. Those are the only two names I trust in a doorman.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You have a budget of like $400 a month.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I'm very flexible on everything else.

jokes.text: Ron's IUD/IOW confusion: Leslie corrects 'IUD Awards' to 'IOW.' Ron: 'No, this portrait is not official in any way. I'm paying for it myself.'
jokes.setup: Ron calls the IOW the 'IUD Awards' (an intrauterine device) while posing for a portrait
jokes.punchline: When corrected, Ron's response addresses only the portrait's official status — he completely ignores the naming error and answers a question nobody asked
jokes.explanation: Ron's IUD slip is a solid if slightly lazy joke (the obvious confusion between similar acronyms). The better joke is Ron's non-sequitur response to the correction — he answers completely the wrong thing, showing he's paying only selective attention. The portrait detail (paying for it himself) adds an absurdist element.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This place has a heated infinity pool, a movie theater, and a wine cellar.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh my god, yes! Where is it?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's in the Arctic Circle and costs $47 million.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dammit. You almost had me.

jokes.text: Ron poses for a portrait and asks Leslie to choose which prop best 'represents women': a pot or a Deputy Director Barbie doll.
jokes.setup: Ron is having an official-ish portrait taken for the IOW award dinner program
jokes.punchline: His options for props representing womanhood are a cooking pot or a Barbie doll — both deeply retrograde choices, presented earnestly
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Ron posing for this portrait with either a pot or a Barbie is funny in its own right, and it works as character comedy — these ARE Ron's sincere best guesses at female symbols. The comedy deepens because he's asking Leslie (who is desperately trying to get this award) to help him pose for it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So I've been studying the investment strategies of some of the most successful entrepreneurs in America. I'm talking about the Kardashians, the Real Housewives, and Jersey Shore cast members. These people have figured out how to turn absolutely nothing into millions of dollars. That's the business model I'm going with.

jokes.text: Leslie interacting with the Deputy Director Barbie: 'Isn't it adorable? She's got a little briefcase, her cell phone. I'm going to help my boss win an award.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is supposed to be arguing with Ron about the award
jokes.punchline: She becomes enchanted by the Barbie and voices it — inadvertently scripting her own subordinate position
jokes.explanation: Deeply on-brand Leslie moment — she starts performing the Barbie's voice and accidentally articulates her own situation. The self-aware irony is funnier because she seems completely unaware of it. Lovely character writing that rewards attention.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We're investing... TWO HUNDRED THOUSAND DOLLARS!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Two. Hundred. Thousand. Dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's two hundred thousand dollars.

jokes.text: Ron's confessional: 'Everything I do is the attitude of an award winner because I've won an award.'
jokes.setup: Leslie accuses Ron of not having the attitude of an award winner (he passed the buck to Donna on the soccer issue)
jokes.punchline: Ron's circular tautological logic — he won an award, therefore everything he does is award-worthy, because he won the award
jokes.explanation: Ron's unflinching self-satisfaction is well-deployed here. The circular logic is a perfect comedic structure and could only work in a confessional where Ron addresses it directly to camera with complete sincerity. Tautological pride is a very Ron Swanson move.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Come on, people! Mark is amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mark! Mark! Mark!

jokes.text: Andy apartment hunting: 'I can afford like 300 bucks a month. I've always wanted a doorman named Ernie. That'd be awesome. Or Kipp.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are looking at apartment listings with his $300/month budget
jokes.punchline: His specific requirement is not space, location, or price — but a doorman named Ernie (or the acceptable alternative, Kipp)
jokes.explanation: Andy's priorities are completely inverted and specifically charming — $300/month but hopes for a doorman, and not just any doorman, but one with a specific name. 'Or Kipp' as the acceptable alternative is perfectly chosen (Kipp is just as old-timey specific). Shows Andy's rich fantasy life totally divorced from his economic reality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look at all these awards I've won!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's... the National Association of Female Business Leaders Award. Sounds like female stuff.

jokes.text: April shows Andy a listing: Tudor mansion, 7 rooms, 4 bathrooms, tennis court, pool, 3-car garage — 'And it's only $20,000 a month. And it's in Chicago.'
jokes.setup: April reads off an increasingly impressive property listing
jokes.punchline: The price is $20,000/month — for someone with $300 — and it's in a different city entirely
jokes.explanation: April is messing with Andy slightly — or completely sincere and helpless at apartment searching. Andy's 'That close! It was almost perfect.' reaction makes it funnier. The joke relies on Andy's response more than the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not sexist. I treat women exactly the same as men.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you literally said women aren't funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's not sexist, that's just an observable fact.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I have proof you respect women. You go to WNBA games.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I go to those games because the fundamentals are sound and there's no three-point line.

jokes.text: Tom's investment pitch at Multipurpose Room F opens with: 'Do any of you have pacemakers or a history of epilepsy? Yes, both. Anybody? No? Both. All right.'
jokes.setup: Tom opens his investment pitch with standard disclaimers
jokes.punchline: He asks about pacemakers and epilepsy, gets an apparent 'yes, both' from someone in the room, completely ignores it, and proceeds
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates perfectly: he asks the standard disclaimer question, someone answers 'yes, both,' Tom says 'All right' and continues — completely indifferent to the safety concern he himself raised. This reveals the disclaimer was pure performance. The 'All right' as a pivot is perfectly economical.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Dorothy Everton Smythe was an absolute trailblazer. She was the first woman to wear pants in public on a Sunday, which was illegal at the time.

jokes.text: Tom's celebrity list: 'Jay-Z. Rihanna. Audrina Patridge. Jon Gosselin. Lady Gaga. Snooki. Are these real people? Cash Warren and Dennis Rodman.'
jokes.setup: Tom is listing celebrities who 'wish they could invest' in his nightclub
jokes.punchline: The list mixes A-listers (Jay-Z, Rihanna) with reality TV footnotes (Audrina Patridge, Jon Gosselin, Snooki) and Kim Kardashian's obscure husband (Cash Warren) — Jerry's interjectory 'Are these real people?' captures the audience's reaction
jokes.explanation: The joke works on the absurdity of the list's composition — Tom equates Jay-Z with Jon Gosselin. Jerry's 'Are these real people?' is the perfect straight-man question. Some of the names are dated (2010 pop culture), which slightly reduces rewatch value. The escalating cheapness of the celebrities is the structure.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Check out this bathroom. The acoustics in here are incredible!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, that's not a priority when choosing an apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Not a priority? April, I need to be able to hear myself sing in the shower. This is non-negotiable.

jokes.text: Tom's pitch with the triple echo: 'For the small price of only one, one, one, thousand, thousand, thousand dollars, dollars, dollars!'
jokes.setup: Tom is revealing the investment amount in his pitch
jokes.punchline: He delivers '$1,000' in a theatrical triple-echo format, as if this makes the ask more impressive or dramatic
jokes.explanation: Tom's showmanship is always excessive relative to what he's actually delivering. The triple echo applied to '$1,000' (a modest amount) makes the grandiosity funnier. It's a visual/performance gag described through text.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna do something today. I don't know what yet, but it's gonna be awesome.

jokes.text: Tom circles the room pointing: 'Mark, I'm talking to you! Donna, I'm talking to you! Jerry! I'm talking to you! Mark! I'm talking to you!'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to generate investment interest among office colleagues
jokes.punchline: He points to Mark twice (and apparently ignores others) — the circling energy is chaotic and the repeat of Mark suggests the loop is breaking down
jokes.explanation: Mainly a performance moment — works better on screen than on page. The repetition of Mark's name (he's already been called out once) implies Tom is panicking and looping. Functional energy gag.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? This place screams my name.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I mean, it literally screams. I think there's a ghost. But also, it screams my name.

jokes.text: Leslie displays her trophy wall: 'Twenty-six certificates, plaques, ribbons, trophies, medals and miscellany certifying that I am the kind of person who deserves recognition for her achievements.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is showing Ron her collection as part of their ongoing award argument
jokes.punchline: The word 'miscellany' at the end of the list, and the entire speech being a meta-description of what an award collection IS, is deeply self-aware for a character who lacks self-awareness
jokes.explanation: 'Miscellany' is a funny word choice in context — the catch-all for things that don't fit categories even in her awards. The visual gag of 26 items on display is strong. The phrasing 'certifying that I am the kind of person who deserves recognition' is circular and very Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so picture this. You're at a club, right? And the DJ is playing all the hits. 'Turn Down for What,' 'Yeah!' You're having a great time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But then you think to yourself, 'You know what would make this better? If I owned this club.' Well, with Rent-a-Swag, that dream can be a reality.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You could be the owner, making all the decisions, getting all the respect, all the glory.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I have the Dorothy Every Time Smurf Girl Trophy for excellence in female stuff.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just showcased her 26 awards
jokes.punchline: Ron describes his single award with maximum name-mangling ('Dorothy Every Time Smurf Girl') and total category dismissal ('female stuff')
jokes.explanation: A callback to Ron's earlier name-mangling (Camp Xena/Athena), now applied to the award itself. 'Dorothy Every Time Smurf Girl' is a brilliantly wrong version of 'Dorothy Everton Smythe' — it's off just enough to be funny without being random. 'Excellence in female stuff' is the perfect deadpan category description from a man who could not care less about the distinctions. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I'm just saying the club has incredible benefits. We're talking premium membership, exclusive events, networking opportunities with the city's most influential people.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Tom, no. Stop.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But Mark, you haven't even heard about the—

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I said no. This is inappropriate.

jokes.text: Ron produces a handwritten certificate acknowledging Leslie should have won, but concluding he's 'going to let her dangle in order to show her that awards are bull crap.'
jokes.setup: Leslie confronts Ron about the award
jokes.punchline: Ron has already prepared a physical document acknowledging this — his anti-award stance has its own award-like formalism
jokes.explanation: The irony of Ron — who hates awards and institutional recognition — producing a formal written document to mock awards is delicious. 'Let her dangle' is a perfect Ron Swanson phrase. The joke works on structure (he's literally made a certificate about refusing a certificate) and character (his tormenting of Leslie while genuinely admiring her). One of the episode's best structural jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I want to be an owner.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, that's great! Yeah, we can make that happen.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: How much is it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, you'd own half of one share.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Come on, Leslie, you know I'm not sexist. I love powerful women.' / Leslie: 'You do attend a shocking number of WNBA games.'
jokes.setup: Ron defends himself against potential sexism accusations
jokes.punchline: Leslie's evidence is that Ron attends a 'shocking number' of WNBA games — an oddly specific and sincere endorsement of women's sports from the most stereotypically masculine character on the show
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The WNBA attendance is unexpected enough to be a genuine surprise, specific enough to feel true, and 'shocking number' implies it's a real dedicated fandom that catches people off guard. This is worldbuilding through comedy — we learn something real about Ron. The joke subverts the 'hypermasculine man is secretly sexist' assumption. Strong originality and near-perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Wait, so they didn't make a mistake?

dialogue.speaker: Tom Haverford
dialogue.line: No, they deliberately chose a man for a women's award.

jokes.text: You do attend a shocking number of WNBA games.
jokes.setup: Ron says he loves powerful women. Leslie responds.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's evidence for Ron's love of powerful women is the WNBA — unexpected, specific, and somehow very right for Ron.
jokes.explanation: This line does so much work with very few words. It reveals an unexpected character detail (Ron, a hyper-masculine libertarian, is a genuine WNBA fan), it validates his claim of loving powerful women with absurd specificity, and 'shocking number' suggests Leslie has noticed this with some degree of puzzlement. Very economical and very quotable. Near-8 for how much it accomplishes.

dialogue.line: Admits women's achievements get no attention

jokes.text: Leslie on Dorothy Everton Smythe: 'She was the first woman in Pawnee to wear pants on a Sunday. She spent four years in jail for that.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is defending the importance of the award by honoring its namesake
jokes.punchline: The feminist pioneer's achievement was wearing pants on a Sunday — four years in jail as consequence — a grimly absurd historical detail about Pawnee's particular brand of backwards conservatism
jokes.explanation: Classic Parks and Rec Pawnee world-building. The specificity of 'pants on a Sunday' and 'four years in jail' makes the absurdity land harder than a more general statement would. Leslie delivers it with complete sincerity which elevates it. It's also darkly funny that the bar for 'trailblazing feminist' in Pawnee is this low.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I appreciate the gesture, but I can't accept an award for women in government. I'm a man.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, just accept it like a man.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: ...that's the entire point I'm making.

jokes.text: The apartment Andy is viewing has a persistent bad smell — 'You can light a match to get rid of that smell.' / Andy: 'I feel really good about this.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are touring a cheap apartment that apparently smells bad enough that the landlord casually mentions lighting matches
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate positive assessment of an apartment that presumably smells terrible and has an ongoing gas issue
jokes.explanation: Andy's optimism in the face of objectively bad circumstances is a reliable character note. The apartment as visual comedy (bad smell, match suggestion) plays better on screen. The joke works mainly through character consistency rather than structural wit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is absolutely ridiculous! Do you know what Ron Swanson said to me? He said women are just as capable as men. Ron Swanson! An actual feminist!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I said no such thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're right, you're worse. You actually meant it.

jokes.text: April on the terrible apartment: 'It screams Andy Dwyer.' / 'And I live nearby. So we could, like, carpool to work or something.' / 'Are you serious?'
jokes.setup: April is theoretically helping Andy find an apartment
jokes.punchline: 'It screams Andy Dwyer' — a perfectly deadpan semi-insult/compliment about a smelly, cheap apartment — followed by her casual reveal that she lives nearby, which is clearly the actual reason she's showing him this place
jokes.explanation: 'It screams Andy Dwyer' is both genuinely funny as an insult and sweet because April means it affectionately. Her reveal that she lives nearby — delivered so casually it almost slips by — shows her feelings for Andy without any sentiment. 'The scream just got louder' as the ambient sound reinforces the joke. Deep character work embedded in a light moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not going to pull any punches.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to extend my punches with my fists.

jokes.text: Jerry: 'Jeez, Tom, if I spend any more than 25 bucks, I gotta ask my wife.' / Tom: 'Jerry, get out.'
jokes.setup: Tom is looking for co-investors among office colleagues
jokes.punchline: Jerry reveals his household financial limit is $25 — Tom immediately dismisses him
jokes.explanation: $25 as the threshold where Jerry needs permission is both characteristically pathetic and endearing. 'Jerry, get out' is the perfect response — no anger, just total immediate dismissal. Fast, clean, works well.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yo, check it out. I'm gonna open a club where we just dance real close and grind on each other all night long. I'll call it 'Pelvic Thrust.' We'll have a DJ booth shaped like a giant butt.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Jean-Ralphio, that sounds like a lawsuit waiting to happen.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Nah nah nah, check out my rap: 'My name is Jean-Ralphio and I'm here to say, I do the pelvic thrust in a major way.' *does inappropriate dance move* Treat yo' self!

jokes.text: Tom's sales pitch to Mark using a fantasy scenario: 'Or we could go to my nightclub and do some dancing.' / Mark: 'I don't think so, man.' / Tom: 'You'd never have to beg for sex again.'
jokes.setup: Tom is pitching Mark on investing by painting a picture of the social benefits
jokes.punchline: Tom escalates from 'dancing' to 'you'd never have to beg for sex again' as a nightclub benefit — an invasive overshare about what Tom thinks Mark's life is like
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'dancing' to 'sex beg' is a classic Tom Haverford move — he assumes everyone's bottom-line motivation is the same as his. Mark's hurt 'I don't beg for sex now' response and Tom's complete indifference ('Forget about that') makes the exchange land cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Donna, Donna, Donna. I got a business opportunity that's gonna change your life.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: You didn't even hear what it is!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I don't care. I hate you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, Donna, that's harsh.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: No it's not. I've hated him since high school.

jokes.text: Mark: 'I don't wanna get into this, really, but I don't beg for sex now.' / Tom: 'Forget about that, Mark. Are you in or out?' / Mark: 'It's just not really my thing.' / Tom: 'Bye, Mark.'
jokes.setup: Mark has rejected Tom's pitch
jokes.punchline: 'Bye, Mark.' — Tom's instant, emotionless dismissal after Mark declines, without any attempt at further persuasion
jokes.explanation: 'Bye, Mark.' is a great economy joke — two words that convey complete indifference to someone who just refused him. Tom doesn't negotiate; he simply moves on. The speed of the pivot is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I only have two generic inspirational lines I reuse in every song. 'Believe in yourself' and 'The sky's the limit.' That's it. That's the whole songbook.

jokes.text: The IOW representative reveals they deliberately chose a man: 'Well, every year, we give it to a woman, and, frankly, nobody cares.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie argue the award should go to Leslie as it's a women's award
jokes.punchline: The IOW admits they gave it to a man precisely because giving it to a woman generates no attention — a women's organization that must exploit sexism to be noticed
jokes.explanation: This is sharp satirical writing. The joke diagnoses a real media paradox — feminist organizations getting attention requires playing by a sexist media's rules. The writing earns this through the setup of the entire episode. The line 'nobody cares' about women winning a women's award is bleak and funny simultaneously. Genuine social commentary wrapped in absurdist sitcom plotting.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie asked me to say some words about why awards are meaningless and corrupt institutions that—actually, you know what? Awards are great. They're wonderful. I love them. I have several at home that I've given myself, and I display them proudly. Leslie, congratulations on your award. You deserve it.

jokes.text: IOW rep: 'But if you give a women's award to a mustachioed, masculine man, such as yourself, well, then, eventually, people take notice.' / Ron: 'I don't want the damn thing.' / IOW rep: 'Well, we're giving it to you. So, you're gonna take it, like a man.'
jokes.setup: The IOW rep is explaining their reasoning for giving a women's award to Ron
jokes.punchline: 'So you're gonna take it, like a man.' — the phrase 'like a man' applied to accepting a women's award, delivered by a feminist organization rep
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best constructed jokes. 'Take it like a man' from a feminist organization awarding a women's prize to an actual man is a perfectly ironic phrase — the language of gender norms deployed by the people supposed to be dismantling them. The writers constructed a situation specifically to land this line. Excellent economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm giving this award away. It's called the Dottie English Whatever.

jokes.text: Ron's outburst: 'The IOW is a bunch of sexist jerks who need to get back in the kitchen where they belong, and leave the real feminist work to actual feminists like Ron Swanson!'
jokes.setup: Ron is outraged that the IOW gave the award to him to exploit media attention
jokes.punchline: He defends Leslie using the most offensive anti-feminist language possible, then claims to be the 'actual feminist' — a man who hates organizations and government defending feminism by telling women to get back in the kitchen
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. Ron defends women's rights using the exact language of women's oppression, then concludes by calling himself the 'actual feminist.' The joke requires all of Ron's prior characterization to work — we need to know he's simultaneously a man's man, Leslie's reluctant defender, and someone who operates by his own moral logic. 'Like Ron Swanson' as the apex of feminist role models is the perfect button. Near-anchor quality for character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you deserve this award.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. Leslie, you take it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I insist. You earned this.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I earned nothing. You're taking it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, please. I'm begging you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You please. I'm begging you.

jokes.text: Leslie's response: 'Now do you see how silly these things are?' / Leslie: 'Unbelievable.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just screamed at the IOW about being sexist jerks while defending Leslie
jokes.punchline: Ron uses his own deranged outburst as an object lesson about awards being silly — Leslie is speechless
jokes.explanation: A functional beat following the strong previous joke. The whiplash from Ron's outburst to him calmly asking 'Now do you see?' is good. Leslie's 'Unbelievable' is the perfect one-word response.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I gave Tom all my money to invest. He's like the Warren Buffay of our friend group.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I want you to rip awards a new a-hole!' / Ron: 'Now we're talking.' / Leslie: 'I won't. I'm gonna push my punches as far as my fists can extend!'
jokes.setup: Leslie, converting to Ron's anti-award stance, wants him to destroy the IOW awards at the ceremony
jokes.punchline: 'Push my punches as far as my fists can extend' — Leslie attempting to say she won't pull punches but mangling the expression into its opposite
jokes.explanation: Leslie's malapropism of 'pull no punches' into 'push my punches as far as my fists can extend' is both stupid and kind of logical — she's conceptually correct but has constructed her own opposite idiom. Ron's 'Now we're talking. Attagirl. Kind of.' is the perfect skeptical endorsement. Good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Donna? What are you doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'm an investor now. I bought in after your pitch.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, you invested? How much?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: More than you.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's pitch to Donna: 'Let's seal this devil's three-way right here, right now. Step one, we buy into this club. Step two, we roll over to the club, either in your Mercedes Benz or my pre-owned Acura Legend. Step three, I dagger you on the dance floor.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is trying to convince Donna to join the investment
jokes.punchline: His three-step plan escalates from business (buy into club) to logistics (whose car) to personal (dagger you on the dance floor) — and 'my pre-owned Acura Legend' is a hilariously specific downgrade from Donna's Mercedes
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's three-step plan is perfectly structured comedy escalation. The progression from business to transportation to seduction ('I dagger you on the dance floor') is the joke's spine. But the real gem is 'pre-owned Acura Legend' — the very specific, decidedly non-luxury car offered as an alternative to a Mercedes. 'Dagger you on the dance floor' as a climactic seduction move, then demonstrated with the bounce song, is committed character absurdism. The 'devil's three-way' framing is also funny.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio breaks into song: 'Just bounce, bounce, bounce, bounce / Now, all the ladies say it / Bounce, bounce, bounce, bounce, bounce'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is describing 'step three' of his plan with Donna
jokes.punchline: He spontaneously performs a terrible club song in the middle of a business meeting, commanding Donna to join in
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio spontaneously performing a club song in a government conference room to close a business deal is peak character comedy. The song itself is hilariously basic ('bounce' repeated). The setup that this is 'step three' of a romantic plan makes the musical performance both expected and perfect.

jokes.text: Donna immediately leaves after Jean-Ralphio's pitch: 'I'm out.' / Tom: 'Why?' / Donna: 'I hate that guy.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just witnessed Jean-Ralphio's disastrous approach
jokes.punchline: Donna's explanation is completely sufficient: 'I hate that guy.' Tom's baffled 'Why?' shows he still doesn't see the problem
jokes.explanation: 'I hate that guy' is economically perfect — no elaboration needed after everything we just saw. Tom's 'Why?' as a genuine question shows his complete lack of self-awareness about his best friend's behavior. Good pacing, clean button on the Jean-Ralphio sequence.

jokes.text: What do you say, sexy? / I'm out. / Why? / I hate that guy.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio finishes his pitch/dance and asks Donna if she's in.
jokes.punchline: Donna immediately withdraws, and when Tom asks why, gives the simple, total, honest response: 'I hate that guy.' Not the deal, not the terms — just pure personal rejection of Jean-Ralphio as a human.
jokes.explanation: 'I hate that guy' is three words that do enormous work. It's the most honest and complete assessment of Jean-Ralphio possible, delivered with no rancor but total finality. Donna's economy of expression here is perfect, and the contrast with Jean-Ralphio's elaborate performance makes it land harder. Highly quotable, great reaction beat.

jokes.text: Ron arrives at the IOW ceremony and is greeted with 'Yay!' from an attendee — Leslie is stopped from following: 'I'm sorry. This area is for award winners only.'
jokes.setup: Ron (who doesn't want the award) is given VIP access; Leslie (who desperately wants it) is blocked
jokes.punchline: The situation's irony is crystallized by the velvet-rope exclusion — the award winner doesn't want to be there; the rightful winner can't get in
jokes.explanation: Situational irony that works without needing dialogue to explain itself. Leslie being physically excluded from the award she earned, while Ron reluctantly enters, completes the episode's central comic tension visually.

jokes.text: Ron to Leslie, excluded from the ceremony: 'Work on the speech. Let's nail these women.' / Leslie: 'You know what I mean. Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Ron is heading in to the feminist award ceremony he'll use to denounce feminist awards
jokes.punchline: 'Let's nail these women' — immediately recognized as wrong — Leslie's 'You know what I mean' and her agreement anyway
jokes.explanation: The quick self-correction is a reliable comedy structure. 'Nail these women' at a feminist awards ceremony lands with appropriate cringe, and Leslie's immediate 'Yeah' after the clarification shows she's too invested to care about the phrasing.

jokes.text: Tom's confessional about his mogul dreams: 'All I want in life is to own a nightclub on every continent, have my own line of upscale sweat suits, and a cologne called Tommy Fresh.'
jokes.setup: Tom is lamenting falling $1,000 short of his investment goal
jokes.punchline: His vision of success: nightclub empire, 'upscale sweat suits' (an oxymoron), and 'Tommy Fresh' cologne — specific, slightly tacky, completely sincere
jokes.explanation: 'Upscale sweat suits' is the detail that makes this great — the cognitive dissonance of 'upscale' and 'sweat suits' is perfectly Tom. 'Tommy Fresh' as a cologne name has the right flavor of aspirational tackiness. The nightclub on every continent is ambitious but dwarfed by the mundane absurdity of the sweat suits.

jokes.text: Andy reveals his two songwriting lines he uses in every song: 'Spread your wings and fly' and 'You deserve to be a champion.'
jokes.setup: Tom doubts Andy's ability to contribute $1,000 to the investment
jokes.punchline: Andy defends his musical credibility by citing the two generic inspirational lines he recycles in all his music — revealing the depth of his craft
jokes.explanation: Andy's songwriting process being two generic lines endlessly recycled is the perfect comedic insight into his artistic ambition vs. his actual output. Both lines are specifically bland — 'Spread your wings and fly' is a cliché, and 'You deserve to be a champion' is aggressively mediocre inspirational content. That he shares them proudly and they apparently constitute his entire catalog is beautifully absurd.

jokes.text: Ron begins his acceptance speech: 'Every award, from the smallest trophy to the Nobel Prize, is nothing more than...' — then 60 seconds of silence before finishing: 'Is nothing more than a great way to honor someone.'
jokes.setup: Ron is supposed to deliver Leslie's speech eviscerating awards as meaningless; the audience expects anti-award rhetoric
jokes.punchline: After a long dramatic pause (clearly spent wrestling with his conscience), Ron pivots and delivers a sincere pro-award speech — the opposite of what was planned
jokes.explanation: The episode's emotional and comedic payoff. The structure is near-perfect: a full minute of silence (represented by the [19:02] to [19:02] gap in the transcript) where Ron genuinely reconsidered. The pivot from 'is nothing more than...' to '...a great way to honor someone' is both a setup/punchline and a sincere character moment. The misdirection works because we expected the anti-award speech, and because Ron's character makes both outcomes plausible. Earned vs. cheap scores high because this is built from the entire episode's setup. One of the episode's top three moments.

jokes.text: Ron presenting the award: 'I would like to present this year's Dottie English Whatever Award to the person who actually deserves it, Leslie Knope.'
jokes.setup: Ron is sincerely giving the award to Leslie
jokes.punchline: His sincere gesture is delivered with 'Dottie English Whatever Award' — yet another wrong version of Dorothy Everton Smythe — making his affection for Leslie coexist with his total indifference to the award's name
jokes.explanation: A callback to Ron's consistent name-mangling that works as both a joke and an emotional beat. 'Dottie English Whatever Award' confirms Ron's total disregard for the institutional details while his action (giving it to Leslie) shows his genuine care for her. The joke rewards the audience for tracking Ron's name mangles throughout the episode. Character integration is near-perfect: this exact combination of sincere generosity and linguistic indifference is uniquely Ron.

jokes.text: Ron and Leslie pass the award back and forth on stage, both insisting the other should have it, ending with Ron: 'Could someone please just take it?' / Crowd member: 'Okay, I'll take it.'
jokes.setup: Ron gives the award to Leslie, Leslie gives it back, they argue on stage
jokes.punchline: The absurd standoff is resolved by a random audience member simply taking the award — neither of them ends up with it
jokes.explanation: A genuinely funny escalation that pays off unexpectedly. The two characters arguing over who should NOT have the award, until a third party resolves it by simply wanting it, is an elegant solution. 'Get off the stage! Yeah!' from the crowd adds a nice button. The award that caused all this strife ends up with nobody involved.

jokes.text: An audience member takes the trophy: 'Okay, I'll take it. Who do I speak to about getting this changed?' / Crowd: 'Get off the stage!'
jokes.setup: Ron asks someone to take the trophy
jokes.punchline: A stranger takes it, immediately tries to redirect it, and the crowd boos her off stage
jokes.explanation: A quick crowd-reaction button for the trophy sequence. Functional punchline — stranger takes trophy, immediately tries to claim it for herself, crowd reacts. Less character-specific than most jokes in this episode but provides a good scene ender.

jokes.text: Ron's final word on awards: 'I still think awards are stupid. But they'd be less stupid if they went to the right people.'
jokes.setup: The award ceremony has concluded with Leslie getting the trophy
jokes.punchline: Ron maintains his stated position while quietly making a concession — but frames the concession in the least complimentary possible way
jokes.explanation: Ron's final thesis is both a callback and a character statement: he holds his position ('awards are stupid') while revealing he cares enough to ensure they go to the right person. 'They'd be less stupid if they went to the right people' is efficient, in-character, and emotionally satisfying. It's Ron's version of saying 'I care about Leslie' without saying anything of the sort. Great episode button.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I'm like Warren Buffay.'
jokes.setup: Andy has given Tom all his money as an investment
jokes.punchline: 'Warren Buffay' — Andy's mispronunciation of Warren Buffett reveals he knows the concept of a famous investor but not the actual name
jokes.explanation: Elegant one-word joke. 'Buffay' as Andy's version of 'Buffett' (and its rhyme with 'buffet') tells you everything about Andy's relationship with knowledge. Two syllables doing a lot of work. Specific to Andy — Chris Pratt's delivery presumably makes this even funnier.

jokes.text: Andy gave Tom his savings: 'You gave Tom all your money?' / Andy: 'Yeah, well, I'm investing. I'm like Warren Buffay.'
jokes.setup: April discovers Andy gave Tom his $1,000
jokes.punchline: Andy compares himself to Warren Buffett but pronounces it 'Buffay' — like a food buffet — completely unaware of the error
jokes.explanation: 'I'm like Warren Buffay' is a great Andy malapropism. The buffet mispronunciation of Buffett is perfectly in-character — Andy has heard the name but never learned to say it. The confidence with which he invokes Warren Buffett while mispronouncing his name as a food service concept is pure Andy Dwyer. High economy (four words does the work) and maximum character integration.

jokes.text: The IOW awards program photo has cropped Leslie out — she's not visible in the photo despite being present
jokes.setup: Leslie has attended the IOW ceremony despite not winning
jokes.punchline: Even in the physical record of the event, Leslie has been erased — she's been cropped out of the photo
jokes.explanation: A sharp visual punchline that crystallizes Leslie's entire relationship with the IOW this episode. 'Figures.' as her response — resigned rather than explosive — is a nice character beat showing her self-awareness in defeat. The visual gag requires the visual medium to fully land but works even in transcript.

jokes.text: Ron and Leslie hang the award in their shared office: 'I have an idea. One, two, three. Two, three.' — implied shared placement
jokes.setup: Neither Ron nor Leslie ended up with the award; Ron suggests an idea for where to put it
jokes.punchline: The implied solution — they mount it together in the shared office — is a warm but funny beat given that neither wanted it to go to the other
jokes.explanation: A warm comedic coda rather than a pure joke. Works as character relationship payoff. The comedy is in the situation — neither of them 'won' but they end up with the award anyway, hanging it together.

jokes.text: Tom at the Snakehole: 'Tom Haverford, part-owner. Let me know if you need anything. Keep this booth warm for me every night. I'm gonna live in this booth.'
jokes.setup: Tom has finally gotten into the Snakehole as a part-owner
jokes.punchline: His triumphant arrival immediately escalates to claiming permanent residency — 'I'm gonna live in this booth'
jokes.explanation: Good character button. Tom's celebration immediately overreaches — part-owner becomes permanent resident in the span of two sentences. Consistent with his character, functional end-of-episode beat.

jokes.text: Donna reveals she bought three shares: 'I bought three shares. Thanks for the tip.'
jokes.setup: Tom is celebrating at the club; Donna appears unexpectedly as an owner
jokes.punchline: Donna — who declined Tom's pitch and left when Jean-Ralphio showed up — bought in independently and on better terms (three shares, not one)
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback and character reveal. Donna didn't reject the investment — she rejected Jean-Ralphio and Tom's sales pitch. She then did the deal her own way, more aggressively than Tom did. 'Thanks for the tip' is a perfect deadpan — she used Tom's information while cutting him out of the negotiation. Strong Donna character moment.

tmdb_overview: Leslie is outraged when Ron wins a "Woman of the Year" award for a project she started. Meanwhile, Tom is desperate to find some money to invest in a local Pawnee club.
insight: Leslie's award obsession drives 61 jokes across 24 minutes—her densest character-comedy showcase yet.
